subject: PCOUNT overestimating abundances for simulated data compared to multinomPois

messages.author: 7d580ad3af7f847b
messages.subject: PCOUNT overestimating abundances for simulated data compared to multinomPois
parts:
Hi UNMARKED Google Members,

 

I simulated data to evaluate the performance of the n-mixture model for repeated visits and the multinomial Poisson model with removal sampling to test the utility of both models for bat ecological studies. I ran multiple scenarios – varying sample size (number of sites), number of visits, and probabilities of detection and population sizes.

 

I found that overall the n-mixture model overpredicted abundances for most of my simulated datasets, whereas, the removal sampling model was accurate in predicting the population size for most variations within a scenario.

 

I did not include covariates in either model, as I wanted to understand how both preformed without additional factors that would affect abundance estimates.

 

Does anyone have a possible explanation why this is happening? Or has anyone else found similar results?

 

Thank you all for your time,

 

Kathryn

messages.subject: Re: PCOUNT overestimating abundances for simulated data compared to multinomPois
parts:
Hi Kathryn, 
Please note...I have very limited experience, but just to add my 2 cents....
During initial evaluation of my study data, I had limited # of sites, but 120 visits (4 time periods over 30 days) and while several models fit, I received unreasonably high abundance estimates with PCount.  Pooling and stacking (discussed in this forum under a different thread) didn't work either, so I ended up taking subsets (3 and 4 day snippets) of the whole data set.  

Of the 32 subsets I created, I was able to obtain only 6 that returned fitted models and gave me decent (reasonable) abundance estimates. While these results, to me, were a bit iffy, just because of the limited amount of data...I learned a lot about the process and so I was happy.  

 Not sure how many sites or visits you have, but this might be the issue.   Drs Royle & Kery discuss the issues of limited sites in chapter 6 I believe, of AHM (part1), and there's also a good article (I'll try to attach) that discusses the fact that increased sites beats increased visits.   Not sure if that helps...I may be way off, so take with a tablespoon of salt.

Victoria

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Re: PCOUNT overestimating abundances for simulated data compared to multinomPois
parts:
Hello again, Kathryn,

for small samples and/or small p, the binomial N-mixture model (Royle, Biometrics, 2004: which is the one you fit when using PCount) is sometimes not identifiable. In these cases, the maximum likelihood estimate is infinity for abundance and 0 for detection (see Biometrics paper by Dennis et al., 2015). In obtaining the estimates, inside of unmarked there is the tuning "parameter" called K, which has to be set to a large value such that the results (i.e., estimates, AIC) no longer change appreciably when you re-run the model with a higher value of K. If we have a data set for which the model is unidentified, then with a finite K, we artificially impose a non-infinity estimate of abundance, but since the "estimates want to go to infinity", we will get abundance estimates that are as high as your value of K allows. But this estimate is flawed, since the real MLE is infinity, and that is meaningless in practice of course

Such identifiability problems can happen with any of the three mixtures for which PCount caters (P, ZIP, NB), but they are especially common for the NB mixture, where in a large screening test with about 140 data sets I found problems in about 25% of the cases in work that I recently submitted as a paper.

To me, your situations sounds exactly like such a case: that for your data sets, the binomial Nmix model is not identifiable. To test this, you ought to re-run all models with much larger value of K (e.g., 1000) and see whether estimates or AIC change.

Best regards  --- Marc
